title: Hello, what's your name?
goal: Greet people at the right time of day, say your name, ask how someone is, and recognize the two ways of greeting: casual and polite.
bekal: greet with *bonjour*, *bonsoir* and *salut*, each in its proper place
say your own name and ask someone else's
use *je suis* and *tu es* to say who you are

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Le premier jour de cours
dialogs.intro: The first day of a French course in Lyon. Two new students sit down next to each other.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bonjour ! Je m'appelle Budi. Et toi ?
lines.id: Hello! My name is Budi. And you?
lines.literal: good-day! I I-call-myself Budi. and you?

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.id: I'm Camille. Nice to meet you!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Nice to meet you too. How are you?

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Ça va bien, merci. Et toi ?
lines.literal: that goes well, thanks. and you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ça va aussi. Tu es française ?
lines.id: I'm fine too. Are you French?
lines.literal: that goes also. you you-are French(fem.)?

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Oui, je suis de Lyon. Et toi, tu es chinois ?
lines.id: Yes, I'm from Lyon. And you, are you Chinese?
lines.literal: yes, I I-am from Lyon. and you, you you-are Chinese?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Non, je suis indonésien. Je suis de Jakarta.
lines.id: No, I'm Indonesian. I'm from Jakarta.
lines.literal: no, I I-am Indonesian(masc.). I I-am from Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thanks a lot! See you tomorrow, Camille.

notes: **Bonjour works all day, and it is compulsory.** In France, walking into a shop or getting into a taxi without saying *bonjour* is considered rude — far ruder than a grammar mistake. Say it first, then get down to business. After about six in the evening, switch to *bonsoir*.
**Salut works both ways, but only with friends.** The same word means "hi" and "bye", just like Italian *ciao*. Don't use it with officials, doctors or older people — use *bonjour* and *au revoir*.

**Je m'appelle is not "my name is".** Literally it is "I call myself". That's why there is no word for "name" in it, and why the question is *comment tu t'appelles* — "how do you call yourself", not "what is your name".
**Moi, c'est Camille** is a shortcut French people use all the time to introduce themselves — more relaxed than *je m'appelle*. Literally "me, it's Camille".

**Enchanté changes its spelling.** A man writes *enchanté*, a woman *enchantée*. They sound exactly the same (ahn-shahn-TAY) — the extra **e** is silent. This is your first taste of a French habit: writing distinctions you can't hear.

**Je can't be dropped.** Unlike Italian or Spanish, French **must** state the subject. *Suis de Lyon* is wrong; it has to be *je suis de Lyon*. The reason is sound: so many verb endings are silent that without the pronoun nothing would tell you who is doing what.

**Comment ça va** is literally "how does it go". The answer reuses the same phrase: *ça va bien*, *ça va*, or if things aren't great, *ça ne va pas très bien*. The polite form is *comment allez-vous ?*

**Nationalities take a small letter.** *français*, *indonésien*, *chinois* — unlike English. Country names keep their capital: *la France*, *l'Indonésie*. The form also follows the speaker's gender: a man is *indonésien*, a woman *indonésienne*.

grammars.title: Être — the verb "to be"
body: The first verb you need to master, and the most irregular verb in all of French. In this unit you only need the first two lines; the rest comes in Unit 3.
after: *es* and *est* sound **exactly the same** (eh). The last letters are silent — and that is not an exception but a general rule of French you'll meet on every page.
*Vous êtes* is run together: voo-ZET, not voo ET. The **s** at the end of *vous* wakes up because the next word starts with a vowel. This is the liaison explained in the pronunciation chapter.

grammars.title: Greeting by time of day and by closeness
body: Two axes, not one. The first is time; the second is how close you are to the person you're talking to.
after: *Bonne nuit* is not an ordinary evening greeting — it is what you say when parting for the night. If you walk into a restaurant at eight in the evening and say it, you've just told everyone to go to bed. The right word is *bonsoir*.
*Bonjour* is said once a day to the same person. Meeting again in the afternoon, a French person will say *rebonjour* — or simply smile.

sections.title: First words to keep in your pocket

blocks.text: The dozen or so words below cover most first-day small talk. Learn them whole; don't take the grammar apart yet.

*S'il te plaît* for friends, *s'il vous plaît* for people you address politely. This *te* vs *vous* difference will come up again and again throughout the course — it is the most common marker of politeness in French.

blocks.title: Tu or vous?
items: **Tu** for friends, family, fellow students, children, and anyone who has invited you to use it.
**Vous** for strangers, officials, shop staff, bosses, and anyone older. *Vous* is also the plural — so the same word means both polite "you" and "you all".
When in doubt, use **vous**. Using *vous* with a friend just sounds stiff; using *tu* with a stranger sounds rude.
If the other person wants to be more casual, they'll say *on peut se tutoyer* — "we can say *tu* to each other".
